## One-Way ANOVA: CRD {#sec-anova-crd}

```{r}
#| label: setup-4-1
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
crd <- read.csv(data_path("pricing_crd.csv"))
crd$strategy <- factor(crd$strategy, levels = c("Regular", "Discount", "Bundle"))
sav <- read.csv(data_path("saving_rate.csv"))
sav$region <- factor(sav$region, levels = c("North", "Northeast", "Central", "South"))

# One-way ANOVA by the correction-factor method, rounded as in the book
anova_hand <- function(y, g) {
  N <- length(y); k <- nlevels(g); Ti <- tapply(y, g, sum); ni <- tapply(y, g, length)
  G <- sum(y); CF <- round(G^2 / N, 4); Syy <- sum(y^2)
  SST <- round(Syy - CF, 4); SSTr <- round(sum(Ti^2 / ni) - CF, 4); SSE <- round(SST - SSTr, 4)
  MSTr <- round(SSTr / (k - 1), 4); MSE <- round(SSE / (N - k), 4)
  list(N = N, k = k, Ti = Ti, ni = ni, G = G, CF = CF, Syy = Syy, SST = SST, SSTr = SSTr,
       SSE = SSE, MSTr = MSTr, MSE = MSE, F = round(MSTr / MSE, 3),
       sumTi2n = sum(Ti^2 / ni))
}
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Explain why we use ANOVA, not many $t$ tests, to compare three or more means.
2. Describe a completely randomized design (CRD) and the assumptions of one-way ANOVA.
3. Calculate the ANOVA table by hand for a small data set.
4. Read the output of `summary(aov(y ~ trt))` in R and write the conclusion.

### Concept

A retail chain wants to compare **three** pricing strategies. Testing each pair
with a $t$ test needs three tests; with five strategies it needs ten. Each test
has a 5% chance of a Type I error, so the chance of at least one false
"significant" result grows quickly. **Analysis of variance (ANOVA)** tests all
the means at once:
$$
H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k \qquad
H_1: \text{at least one } \mu_i \text{ is different}
$$

In a **completely randomized design (CRD)** the treatments (here, pricing
strategies) are assigned to experimental units (stores) completely at random.

The idea of ANOVA is to split the total variation in the data into two parts:

- variation **between** the treatment means (treatment sum of squares, SSTr)
- variation **within** the treatments (error sum of squares, SSE)

If the treatment means are really equal, the between-treatment variation is only
random noise, about the same size as the within-treatment variation. The ratio
of the two mean squares is an $F$ statistic, as in Section 3.5.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crd-dots
#| fig-cap: "Weekly sales (hundred units) of 15 stores under three pricing strategies; lines show treatment means"
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
means <- aggregate(sales ~ strategy, crd, mean)
ggplot(crd, aes(strategy, sales)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7, position = position_jitter(width = 0.06, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = means, aes(ymin = sales, ymax = sales), width = 0.35, linewidth = 0.8,
                colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Pricing strategy", y = "Weekly sales")
```

### Formulas and Conditions

**Assumptions:** independent random samples (units assigned at random); each
population is normal; all populations have the same variance $\sigma^2$.

With $k$ treatments, $n_i$ observations in treatment $i$, $N = \sum n_i$,
treatment totals $T_i$ and grand total $G$:

| Quantity | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Correction factor | $\text{CF} = G^2/N$ |
| Total SS | $\text{SST} = \sum y^2 - \text{CF}$ |
| Treatment SS | $\text{SSTr} = \sum \dfrac{T_i^2}{n_i} - \text{CF}$ |
| Error SS | $\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr}$ |

**ANOVA table**

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Treatments | $k-1$ | SSTr | $\text{MSTr} = \dfrac{\text{SSTr}}{k-1}$ | $F_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\text{MSTr}}{\text{MSE}}$ |
| Error | $N-k$ | SSE | $\text{MSE} = \dfrac{\text{SSE}}{N-k}$ | |
| Total | $N-1$ | SST | | |

**Critical region:** $F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha,\,k-1,\,N-k}$. The ANOVA $F$
test is always **right-sided**: only a large between-treatment variation is
evidence against $H_0$.

**Decision:** in this chapter we decide with the p-value: reject $H_0$ if
p-value $< \alpha$. The p-value is printed by R in the column `Pr(>F)`.

**In R:** `summary(aov(y ~ trt))`. The row named after the treatment is the
treatment row and `Residuals` is the error row.

```{r}
#| label: ex-4-1
A <- anova_hand(crd$sales, crd$strategy)
oa <- summary(aov(sales ~ strategy, data = crd))[[1]]
```

### Example

**Example 4.1.1.** A retail chain randomly assigns three pricing
strategies (Regular, Discount, Bundle) to 15 similar stores, 5 stores each, and
records weekly sales in hundreds of units:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-crd
#| tbl-cap: "Weekly sales (hundred units) under three pricing strategies"
wide <- data.frame(Strategy = levels(crd$strategy),
                   Sales = sapply(levels(crd$strategy), function(l) paste(crd$sales[crd$strategy == l], collapse = ", ")),
                   Total = as.vector(A$Ti), Mean = as.vector(A$Ti / A$ni))
knitr::kable(wide, row.names = FALSE, align = "llcc")
```

At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean weekly sales differ among the three strategies.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

$k$ = `r A$k`, $N$ = `r A$N`, $G$ = `r A$G`, $\sum y^2$ = `r big(A$Syy, 0)`.

$$
\text{CF} = \frac{`r A$G`^2}{`r A$N`} = `r num(A$CF)`
$$
$$
\text{SST} = `r big(A$Syy, 0)` - `r num(A$CF)` = `r num(A$SST)`
$$
$$
\text{SSTr} = \frac{`r A$Ti[1]`^2 + `r A$Ti[2]`^2 + `r A$Ti[3]`^2}{5} - `r num(A$CF)` = `r num(A$sumTi2n)` - `r num(A$CF)` = `r num(A$SSTr)`
$$
$$
\text{SSE} = `r num(A$SST)` - `r num(A$SSTr)` = `r num(A$SSE)`
$$

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Strategy | `r A$k - 1` | `r num(A$SSTr)` | `r num(A$MSTr)` | `r fmt(A$F, 3)` |
| Error | `r A$N - A$k` | `r num(A$SSE)` | `r num(A$MSE)` | |
| Total | `r A$N - 1` | `r num(A$SST)` | | |

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu_R = \mu_D = \mu_B$ $\quad H_1:$ at least one mean is different

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $F_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{`r num(A$MSTr)`}{`r num(A$MSE)`} = `r fmt(A$F, 3)`$, df = (`r A$k - 1`, `r A$N - A$k`)

**Step 4: p-value.** From the R output below, p-value = `r fmt(oa[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)`.

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(oa[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` <
$\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the mean weekly sales are not all
equal across the three pricing strategies at the 0.05 level of significance.
Section 4.2 shows how to find which strategies differ.
:::

### Reading R Output

```{r}
#| label: r-data-crd
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(grp_code("strategy", levels(crd$strategy), each = 5), vec_code("sales", crd$sales))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-crd
#| echo: !expr show_code
summary(aov(sales ~ strategy))
```

| Output | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `strategy` row | treatment: df $= k-1$, SSTr, MSTr, $F_{\text{cal}}$, p-value |
| `Residuals` row | error: df $= N-k$, SSE, MSE |
| `Pr(>F)` | p-value |
| `***`, `**`, `*` | significance codes; we use the p-value itself |

R does not print the Total row; add the other two rows to get it
(df = `r A$N - 1`, SS = `r num(A$SST)`).

```{r}
#| label: yt-4-1
B <- anova_hand(sav$saving, sav$region)
ob <- summary(aov(saving ~ region, data = sav))[[1]]
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 4.1.1

The household saving rate (% of income) of 4 randomly selected households in
each of four regions is recorded:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sav
knitr::kable(data.frame(Region = levels(sav$region),
                        `Saving rate` = sapply(levels(sav$region), function(l) paste(sav$saving[sav$region == l], collapse = ", ")),
                        Total = as.vector(B$Ti), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

$\sum y^2$ = `r big(B$Syy, 0)`. Some values in the R output below are hidden (`____`).

(a) Complete the ANOVA table by hand.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean saving rate differs among the regions.
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-data-sav
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(grp_code("region", levels(sav$region), each = 4), vec_code("saving", sav$saving))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-4-1
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| eval: false
summary(aov(saving ~ region))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-4-1-out
saving <- sav$saving; region <- sav$region
mask_print(summary(aov(saving ~ region)),
           list(c("^region", 2), c("^region", 3), c("^region", 4), c("^Residuals", 3)))
```

::: {.workspace table="anova" rows="Region,Error,Total" lines="8"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 4.1.1"}
**(a)** $G$ = `r B$G`, CF $= `r B$G`^2/`r B$N` = `r num(B$CF)`$,
SST $= `r B$Syy` - `r num(B$CF)` = `r num(B$SST)`$,
SSTr $= (`r paste(B$Ti, collapse = "^2 + ")`^2)/4 - `r num(B$CF)` = `r num(B$SSTr)`$,
SSE $= `r num(B$SSE)`$.

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Region | `r B$k - 1` | `r num(B$SSTr)` | `r num(B$MSTr)` | `r fmt(B$F, 3)` |
| Error | `r B$N - B$k` | `r num(B$SSE)` | `r num(B$MSE)` | |
| Total | `r B$N - 1` | `r num(B$SST)` | | |

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_N = \mu_{NE} = \mu_C = \mu_S \quad H_1:$ at least one mean is different

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r num(B$MSTr)`/`r num(B$MSE)` = `r fmt(B$F, 3)`$, df = (`r B$k - 1`, `r B$N - B$k`)

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(ob[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(ob[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject
$H_0$. That is, the mean saving rates are not all equal across the four regions
at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Hypotheses | $H_0: \mu_1 = \cdots = \mu_k$; $H_1$: at least one $\mu_i$ different |
| Sums of squares | $\text{CF} = G^2/N$; $\text{SST} = \sum y^2 - \text{CF}$; $\text{SSTr} = \sum T_i^2/n_i - \text{CF}$; $\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr}$ |
| df | treatments $k-1$; error $N-k$; total $N-1$ |
| Test statistic | $F_{\text{cal}} = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$, df $= (k-1,\ N-k)$ |
| Decision | reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$ |
| R | `summary(aov(y ~ trt))` |

### Exercises

**4.1.1** Complete the ANOVA table for a CRD with 4 treatments and 6 units per
treatment. The p-value is `r fmt(pf(4.5, 3, 20, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)`. State the
decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Treatments | (a) | 54.0 | (c) | (e) |
| Error | (b) | 80.0 | (d) | |
| Total | 23 | 134.0 | | |

::: {.answer title="Exercise 4.1.1"}
(a) $k - 1 = 3$; (b) $N - k = 24 - 4 = 20$; (c) $54.0/3 = 18$; (d) $80.0/20 = 4$;
(e) $F_{\text{cal}} = 18/4 = 4.500$.
p-value = `r fmt(pf(4.5, 3, 20, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we
reject $H_0$. That is, the treatment means are not all equal at the 0.05 level
of significance.
:::

**4.1.2** Explain why a researcher comparing five investment funds should use
ANOVA rather than ten separate two-sample $t$ tests.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 4.1.2"}
Each $t$ test has a 5% chance of a Type I error. With ten tests the chance of
at least one false significant result is much larger than 5%. ANOVA tests all
five means in one test at $\alpha$ = 0.05.
:::
